chapters.title: Chapter 5: Analysing Performance Like a Manager

lessons.title: Key Ratios for Non Finance Managers: Margins, ROCE and Working Capital Days

children.text: A ratio is just a question written as arithmetic. Managers are handed dozens of them and remember none, because nobody says what question each one answers.

There are only four questions worth asking about any business. Is it profitable? Does it use its assets well? Can it pay its bills? Can it survive its debt? Every ratio in this lesson belongs to one of those four, and you need about eight of them in total.

body.text: A single ratio means nothing. A ratio compared with last year, with the plan, or with a competitor in the same industry means everything.

children.text: The Four Families

body.caption: Eight ratios that cover almost every question

cells: Stable or rising against last year
Compared only within the same industry
Comfortably above the cost of borrowing
Higher means more sales per rupee invested
Inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days
Shorter than last year, and than peers
Judged against how predictable cash flows are
Above 4 is comfortable, below 2 is fragile

body.text: Benchmarks travel badly across industries. A software firm with a current ratio of 3 and no debt is normal. A grocery retailer with a current ratio of 0.8 and negative working capital is not in trouble, it is simply paid by customers before it pays suppliers. Compare a company with itself over time and with its own industry, never with a textbook number.

children.text: ROCE: The One Ratio to Take Away

If a manager learns a single ratio beyond margin, make it return on capital employed. It answers the question the board actually asks: for every rupee tied up in this business, how much operating profit does it produce?

body.caption: Capital employed is equity plus borrowings, or equivalently total assets minus current liabilities

children.text: Kesari Foods earned operating profit of ₹6 crore. Its capital employed is net worth of ₹21 crore plus borrowings of ₹13 crore, which is ₹34 crore. The other route, total assets of ₹48 crore less current liabilities of ₹13.5 crore, gives ₹34.5 crore. Either way, ROCE is about 17.5%.

stats.label: ROCE
stats.context: ₹6 crore operating profit on ₹34 crore of capital employed

stats.label: Cost of borrowing
stats.context: Pre-tax, on the term loan and cash credit

stats.label: Spread
stats.context: The business earns more than its funding costs

stats.label: Asset turnover
stats.context: ₹50 crore of revenue on ₹48 crore of assets

body.text: The comparison that matters is ROCE against the cost of funding. A business earning 17.6% on capital that costs 11% is creating value with every rupee it invests. A business earning 9% on capital that costs 11% destroys value as it grows, which is how companies expand their way into distress while reporting profits the whole time.

body.title: Compute ROCE
body.prompt: A Rajkot engineering company reports operating profit of ₹21 crore. Its net worth is ₹80 crore and total borrowings are ₹40 crore. What is its ROCE, in percent?
body.explanation: Capital employed = ₹80 crore + ₹40 crore = ₹120 crore. ROCE = ₹21 crore ÷ ₹120 crore = 17.5%. If the company borrows at 10%, every rupee it puts to work earns a healthy spread over what the money costs.

children.text: Return on equity can be split into three parts, a decomposition finance teams call DuPont analysis. It shows where a return actually comes from.
Return on equity equals net margin, times asset turnover, times the equity multiplier, where the multiplier is total assets divided by net worth.
Net margin at Kesari Foods:
₹3.7 crore ÷ ₹50 crore = 7.4%. This is the pricing and cost lever.
Asset turnover:
₹50 crore ÷ ₹48 crore = 1.04 times. This is the efficiency lever, how hard the assets work.
Equity multiplier:
₹48 crore ÷ ₹21 crore = 2.29 times. This is the leverage lever.

Multiply them: 7.4% × 1.04 × 2.29 = about 17.6%, which is exactly ₹3.7 crore ÷ ₹21 crore. The value of the split is diagnostic. Two companies can report the same return on equity, one by earning fat margins and the other by borrowing heavily. Only the first is genuinely operating well.
Efficiency and Liquidity in Practice
Working capital days came up in Lesson 3.2. The liquidity ratios are their balance sheet cousins, and they are what a bank looks at before renewing your cash credit limit.

body.latex: \text{Current ratio} = \frac{\text{Current assets}}{\text{Current liabilities}} \qquad \text{Quick ratio} = \frac{\text{Current assets} - \text{Inventories}}{\text{Current liabilities}}
body.caption: Kesari Foods: 22.0 ÷ 13.5 = 1.63, and (22.0 - 7.0) ÷ 13.5 = 1.11

children.text: The quick ratio strips out inventory because stock is the hardest current asset to turn into cash quickly. A company with a comfortable current ratio and a weak quick ratio is holding its liquidity in the warehouse, which is only liquidity if somebody wants the stock.

body.title: The stricter test
body.textWithBlank: The quick ratio is the current ratio with ___ removed from current assets, because it is the slowest to convert into cash.
body.explanation: Inventory may take months to sell, and in a downturn it sells only at a discount. The quick ratio asks whether the company could meet its short-term obligations without relying on that.

body.title: Pick the right ratio
body.question: Your CEO asks whether the new warehouse and the extra fleet bought last year are actually earning their keep. Which ratio speaks to that most directly?
body.explanation: ROCE measures operating profit against the capital tied up in the business, so new assets that do not generate proportionate profit pull it down immediately. Gross margin would not move at all, since the warehouse and fleet sit below gross profit.

children.text: Two Real Companies, Same Four Questions

Here are the FY25 numbers for Britannia Industries and Infosys, built from the figures shown on screener.in. Read across the rows and the difference between a biscuit maker and a software firm becomes obvious.

cells: Software converts more of each rupee into profit
Before depreciation and interest, on screener's basis
Both as reported on screener.in, and both exceptional because neither needs heavy capital
Not meaningful, there is almost no debt
Interest is a rounding error at both

children.text: Britannia's ROCE of 53% is worth checking by hand, because doing so shows where it comes from. Operating profit after depreciation is about ₹2,863 crore, and capital employed is about ₹5,603 crore, being net worth of ₹4,356 crore plus borrowings of ₹1,247 crore. That gives roughly 51%, close to the reported figure, with the small gap arising because published ratios often use average rather than year-end capital. Either way, a biscuit business that earns about half its capital back every year in operating profit is not normal manufacturing. It is the result of brands, distribution and outsourced production.

columns.label: Ways to raise ROCE
points: Raise price or cut cost, lifting operating profit
Sell more from the same assets, raising turnover
Release working capital, shrinking capital employed
Exit or sell assets that earn below the cost of capital

columns.label: Ways managers accidentally lower it
points: Build capacity well ahead of demand
Let receivables and inventory drift upward with growth
Chase revenue at discounts that thin the margin
Keep a loss-making product line alive because it carries overhead

body.label: screener.in ratio tables
body.description: Every company page shows ten years of margins, ROCE, ROE, debtor days, inventory days and working capital days. The ten-year trend of a single ratio is far more informative than this year's value.

body.title: High margin, poor return
body.scenario: You run a business unit at a Chennai industrial products company. Your unit has the best operating margin in the group at 22%, against a company average of 14%. At the annual review, the CFO says your unit has the worst ROCE, at 9%, against a group average of 19%, and that it will not get funding for expansion until this improves.
body.prompt: How is a high margin business the worst on ROCE, and what would you do about it?
body.modelAnswer:
How both can be true:
1. ROCE is operating profit divided by capital employed. A high margin unit can still be the worst on ROCE if it is carrying far more capital per rupee of sales than the others.
2. The likely culprits are a large asset base running below capacity, heavy inventory because the unit makes to stock rather than to order, long receivable days because customers are large and slow, or land and buildings sitting on the books unused.
3. The arithmetic to run first: revenue ÷ capital employed for my unit and for the group. If my asset turnover is 0.4 against a group figure of 1.3, the gap is efficiency, not profitability.
What I would do, in order:
4. Attack working capital first, because it is the fastest and needs no capital approval. Cut receivable days, clear slow-moving stock even at a discount, renegotiate supplier terms. Every rupee released reduces capital employed directly.
5. Raise utilisation of the existing assets: add a shift, take contract manufacturing work for another unit, or consolidate production into fewer lines.
6. Identify assets that earn nothing. Idle land, an unused warehouse or obsolete machines can be sold or sublet, which lifts ROCE from the denominator side.
7. Review the product mix. A high margin product that consumes enormous working capital may earn less per rupee of capital than a lower margin product that turns over quickly.
What to take back to the CFO:
8. A ROCE bridge showing the current 9%, the effect of each action, and the resulting figure, with timelines.
9. A request that the expansion case be judged on incremental ROCE, since new capacity at group-average turnover would improve the unit's position rather than worsen it.

body.title: Build your own ratio sheet
steps: Take three years of P&L and balance sheet figures for your company or a competitor.
Compute the eight ratios in the table above for each year.
Mark which ones improved and which worsened, and write one sentence on each move.
Compute ROCE and compare it against your company's average borrowing cost.
Split return on equity into margin, asset turnover and leverage to see which lever is doing the work.
Repeat for one listed competitor, and bring the comparison to your next planning meeting.

cards.definition: Operating profit divided by capital employed. How much profit each rupee of capital produces.
Net worth plus borrowings, or equivalently total assets minus current liabilities.
Revenue divided by total assets. How hard the asset base works.
Current assets divided by current liabilities. A short-term solvency check.
Current assets less inventories, divided by current liabilities. The stricter liquidity test.
Splitting return on equity into net margin, asset turnover and leverage to locate the source of the return.
The gap between ROCE and the cost of capital. Positive spread creates value, negative destroys it.

points: Every useful ratio answers one of four questions: profitability, efficiency, liquidity or solvency.
ROCE is the single most useful ratio for a manager, because it links profit to the capital tied up to earn it.
Compare ROCE with the cost of borrowing. Growth only creates value when the spread is positive.
Return on equity splits into margin, asset turnover and leverage, and only the first two reflect operating skill.
The quick ratio strips out inventory, because stock is liquidity only if someone wants it.
Ratios mean nothing in isolation. Compare across years and within the same industry.

body.text: Kesari Foods, the Rajkot engineering company and the Chennai business unit are fictional. Britannia and Infosys figures are FY25 consolidated numbers as reported on screener.in. Ratios such as ROCE vary slightly depending on whether year-end or average capital employed is used, so a figure you compute by hand may not match a published one exactly. Nothing here is investment advice.
